doc.title: Jerry Gordon interviewed by Monk Rowe and Christian Goodwillie, via Zoom, June 30, 2021

chapter: Selling the store and founding Evidence
title: Producing new recordings: Melvin Taylor
summary: Gordon explains how licensing European recordings led to Melvin Taylor and his first new Evidence recording.

bands.name: Melvin Taylor and the Slack Band

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Record labels, producers and the business of making albums

blocks.x: Did you find yourself eventually helping to produce new recordings? Was that part of your goal with Evidence Records?

It was never my goal. I’ll tell you why that happened. Good question, Monk. I had made great deals in France and Germany and eventually Japan. I had great deals with King Records and other Japanese labels. I got Toshiko Akiyoshi recordings that way that were not out here. So I was happy doing all that. And then I put out one guy who was particularly and just so the listeners know, I wasn’t really licensing French and German and Japanese artists, these were all recordings by American artists that had been made by foreign companies. Now I wasn’t the first to license these, there were plenty of labels who were licensing from countries outside the United States, but I really went at it. I really went after it. One of the artists that I had the opportunity to issue his records was a © Fillius Jazz Archive -12-

guitarist named Melvin Taylor, and I am going to answer your question. I’m going to answer it through a discussion of Melvin Taylor. Melvin Taylor was from Chicago and he used to play in a club that’s still active and very hip and that’s called Rosa’s Lounge. He did not go on tours of the United States. He didn’t really play at other clubs in Chicago. He didn’t come into New York. He didn’t do that. He had a once a week gig at Rosa’s Lounge, this guitarist Melvin Taylor. And he was extremely popular there because he was a bluesy, electric guitarist, not rock he was playing blues but it was rock influenced. And I had to issue — and the only time that Melvin Taylor would leave Chicago and play elsewhere is every summer. The owners of the French, two French labels that I had licensed from, these blues records, they were also promoters. A lot of the labels in Europe were owned and started by promoters who had brought in American artists to tour Europe. And while they were there they would bring them into the studio one day, record them you know, and that was it. And that’s why so many European labels were owned by, you know, tour promoters. So Melvin Taylor is in Chicago every week except during the summer, they put him on tour of Europe. They took care of everything, everything was organized for Melvin. And he did that and he had become very very very popular in France. So I had these Melvin Taylor CDs that I had put out in the United States for the first time, but yeah, they were re-issues. They were licenses from these French labels. And the reviews — I actively tried to promote these records and get reviews in the press. And Melvin was getting all these great reviews. People were really loving him. He was like a black Stevie Ray Vaughan. And the reviews, one day I’m reading the reviews — we had a clipping service or the publications would send us reviews. And one day I’m reading this review. “This guy is really great. When is a big label going to sign this guy already?” And I read that and I went oh my God — that second. It was instantaneous. Someone’s going to sign this guy, it really should be me. So that’s what happened. The very first record that was a new recording for Evidence was Melvin Taylor and the Slack Band. And that was one of the biggest records I ever had, bigger than most of my jazz records, huge. It was a big record.
